• What is HTML and why it matters for web development

• Course learning goals

• Structure of the upcoming lessons

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Alex, and today we’re kicking off our journey into HTML—the building blocks of every web page you’ll create.
First, let’s talk about what HTML actually is and why it matters for web development.
HTML gives structure to web content, letting browsers know where headings, paragraphs, images, and links belong. Without it, a page would just be a jumble of text.
Our learning goals for this course are simple: you’ll be able to write clean HTML, create a basic web page layout, and understand how to connect HTML with CSS and JavaScript later on.
We’ll move through a series of short lessons—starting with tags and elements, then building a personal homepage, adding forms, and finally publishing your site.
That’s the roadmap. Keep your questions coming, and let’s build something great together.

elements.content:
• DOCTYPE declaration

• <html>, <head>, <title>, <body> tags

• Simple "Hello World" example

<!DOCTYPE html>

<html>

<head><title>Hello</title></head>

<body>Hello World</body>

</html>

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into the basic structure of an HTML document. This is the foundation for every web page you’ll build.

First, we need a DOCTYPE declaration. It tells the browser that we’re writing an HTML5 document. Then we have the core tags: <html>, <head>, and <body>. Inside <head> we place the <title> tag, which defines the page title shown in the browser tab.

Here’s a simple example—a complete, minimal HTML page that displays a “Hello World” message. Notice how each tag opens and closes properly, and the text we want to show appears inside the <body> section.
Make sure you include every opening and closing tag exactly as shown; missing even one will cause the page to break.
Now that we’ve covered the essential structure, you can start creating your own HTML files by following this template. Great job, and let’s move on to adding more content in the next slide!

elements.content:
• Heading tags h1–h6 define hierarchy

• <p> wraps regular text

• Use headings to structure content

<h1>Main Title</h1>
<h2>Section Title</h2>
<p>This is a paragraph of text.</p>
<h3>Subsection</h3>
<p>Another paragraph.</p>

actions.text: Alright, let's dive into headings and paragraphs in HTML. These two elements are the building blocks for structuring any web page.

First, notice the bullet points here. Heading tags from h1 to h6 create a hierarchy—from the main title down to sub‑sections. The paragraph tag

is used for regular blocks of text.

Now, look at this code example. It shows an h1 for the main title, followed by h2 and h3 headings to break the content into sections, and each paragraph is wrapped in

tags. Remember, the higher the number, the less important the heading, so screen readers and SEO understand the page structure.

To recap, use h1–h6 to outline your page hierarchy and

for normal text. This simple structure makes your HTML clear and accessible.

• Nested list example

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I'm Alex, and today we're diving into HTML list structures—both ordered and unordered.
First, let's look at an ordered list, which uses the <ol> tag. Each item gets a number automatically, making it perfect for step‑by‑step instructions.
Next, here's an unordered list created with the <ul> tag. The items are marked with bullet points, ideal for grouping related ideas without implying order.
You can also nest lists inside one another to create hierarchical structures—just place a new <ol> or <ul> inside a <li> element.
That covers the basics of ordered and unordered lists. Feel free to try adding your own items in the lab, and we'll review your code together shortly.

elements.content:
• Table container <table>

• Rows <tr>, header cells <th>, data cells <td>

• Simple 2×2 table example

actions.text: Hi everyone, I'm Alex. Today we're going to learn how to create tables in HTML so you can display data clearly on your web pages.

First, the table itself starts with the <table> tag, which acts as the container. Inside it, each row is marked with <tr>. Within a row, header cells use <th> and regular data cells use <td>. These are the building blocks of any HTML table.

Here's a simple example of a 2 × 2 table. Notice how we open the <table>, add a <tr> for the first row, place <th> elements for the headers, then another <tr> with <td> cells for the data. This structure will render a neat grid in the browser.
Remember, you can add as many rows and columns as you need—just keep nesting <tr> and <td>/<th> inside the <table> element.

actions.topic: How might you use a table to show a weekly schedule?
actions.prompt: Think about the rows and columns you would need.

elements.content:
• <form> element with action attribute

• Common controls: <input>, <label>, <textarea>, <button>

• Example: simple contact form

<form action="/submit" method="post">

  <label for="name">Name:</label>

  <input type="text" id="name" name="name">

  <label for="msg">Message:</label>

  <textarea id="msg" name="msg"></textarea>

  <button type="submit">Send</button>

</form>

actions.text: Alright, let's dive into Forms Basics. This section will cover the core elements you need to build a simple contact form.

First, the <form> tag itself. The action attribute tells the browser where to send the form data when the user clicks submit, and the method attribute (usually "post") determines how that data is transmitted.
Inside a form you’ll typically use common controls like <input> for text fields, <label> to describe them, <textarea> for longer messages, and <button> to trigger submission.
Here’s a quick example of a contact form snippet. Notice how each input has a matching label, and the form’s action points to "/submit" with method="post".
That’s the essential building blocks for HTML forms. Once you’re comfortable with these elements, you can start adding validation and styling to create polished user experiences.

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into Semantic HTML and some good coding practices that make our pages more accessible and easier to maintain.
First, we use semantic elements like header, nav, main, section, article, and footer. These tags tell browsers and assistive technologies what each part of the page represents.
Next, give your headings clear hierarchy and always add alt attributes to images. This helps screen readers and improves SEO.
Finally, keep your code nicely indented. Clean indentation makes it easier for anyone—including future you—to read and update the markup.

questions.analysis: A unordered list (ul) is the standard way to group navigation links, typically placed inside a nav element. The nav element itself provides the semantic wrapper, but the list structure is ul.

questions.analysis: Option C uses article to represent the post, header to group title and author, and a paragraph for the main content—fully semantic. Option A lacks a header wrapper for the author, B uses span (non‑semantic) for author, and D relies on div with classes only.

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's dive into Quiz 2: Putting It All Together. This short quiz will let you apply what we've just covered about choosing the right HTML tags and spotting semantic markup. Read each question carefully, and remember the key ideas we discussed earlier.

For Q1, think about the tag that signifies the primary heading of a page—it's the one search engines and screen readers look for first. For Q2, focus on elements that give meaning to the structure of an article, rather than just styling. Q3 is about the best container for a list of navigation links, and Q4 asks you to pick the most semantically correct combination for a blog post, including a header for the title and author.

Common pitfalls to watch out for: using <div> or <span> when a semantic element exists, mixing up <header> with <title>, and forgetting to wrap navigation links inside a <nav> or list element. If you choose the options that use <article>, <header>, <section>, <aside>, and proper list tags, you're on the right track.
